rationale: Well-designed large-scale field and online RCTs, careful inference, credible mechanisms, and timely topic give the study standing in the top decile of recent political-economy work. Minor limits in generalizability and data availability temper a perfect score.

Main claims are clearly stated and directly tested with randomized treatments; effects are replicated across settings and robustness checks reported. Remaining uncertainty about external validity and longer-run impacts prevents an even higher score.

Impressive sample size (≈880k voters), cluster-randomized design, preregistration, placebo controls, 2SLS for varying take-up, extensive robustness. Some potential spillovers and measurement limits acknowledged but not fully resolved.

Provides rare causal evidence on misperceptions sustaining authoritarian support, informing both theory and practice. Adds to persuasion and democracy literatures with novel Turkish context. Contribution is substantial though not wholly paradigm-shifting.
Paper is long yet well-structured; arguments follow logically from results, figures and appendices are clear. Some redundancy and heavy jargon slightly reduce accessibility.
Study registered; IRB approvals and treatment materials shared. Code/data availability not yet complete (voter rolls proprietary, online data partly restricted), limiting full reproducibility.

Understanding demand for democracy under authoritarianism is central to global governance priorities; findings have policy implications beyond Turkey, especially for information interventions in similar regimes.

Influential theorists provide novel synthesis of AI, automation, Baumol effects and singularity within growth theory. Strong conceptual contribution but limited empirical validation and open-science practices temper score.
Paper makes clear, appropriately caveated claims and offers formal models; empirical sections illustrative, not definitive. Evidence supports theory qualitatively but lacks rigorous testing.
Analytical growth models well-specified, build on Zeira/Acemoglu frameworks; assumptions explicit. Empirical illustrations descriptive; robustness and endogeneity largely unaddressed.
Introduces complementary lenses (automation + Baumol) shaping AI–growth debate; sets research agenda, widely cited, high potential impact on macro & policy discourse.
Writing lucid; questions, assumptions, and derivations transparent; arguments logically coherent with clear figures; minor complexity but accessible to field.
Working paper freely available but no code or data release; models reproducible in principle, empirical data publicly sourced yet no replication materials or pre-registration.
Addresses AI’s long-run growth impacts, income distribution, and policy—issues central to global economic planning and developing-country convergence.

Large‐scale RCT with saturation variation to estimate general‐equilibrium effects of seasonal migration. Design, data richness, and analyses are well above field median; minor concerns on external validity, wage instrument strength in some subsamples, and heavy reliance on self-reported income prevent top-decile rating.

Main claims (migration spillovers, wage increases, food-price effects) clearly stated and generally supported by randomized variation and multiple data sources. Robustness checks extensive. Some secondary claims (employer profits, welfare) less precisely estimated.

Innovative saturation experiment, high-frequency surveys, IV analysis, clustered SEs, balance & robustness shown. Credible identification; small weaknesses: partial first-stage strength for non-ag wages, self-report measurement error, limited discussion of missing data.
First experimental evidence on general-equilibrium effects of internal migration; informs development theory and policy on labor mobility. Likely to shape subsequent research and scale-up decisions.
Paper is long but logically structured; theoretical framework, hypotheses, and results aligned. Some sections dense; key results occasionally buried in appendices, and figures could be clearer.
Trial registered; appendices include extensive tables. However, replication code and raw data availability not stated in working-paper version; unclear if publicly archived.
Addresses seasonal poverty affecting hundreds of millions; findings pertinent to policies in South Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, China. Applicability outside agrarian lean-season contexts needs caution.

Large, well-designed nationwide RCT on social-media health messaging; careful causal identification; clear writing. Offline effects modest and partly self-reported, open-science weaker, but overall among stronger recent applied econ/dev papers.
Online diffusion claims tightly backed by randomization. Offline belief/behavior claims presented as ‘suggestive’; authors are mostly cautious, though some generalisations exceed evidence strength.

Multi-level randomized design, use of Poisson models, clustering, RI p-values, double-post LASSO. Design cleverly addresses endorsement vs reach. Limitations: self-report outcomes, multiple hypothesis burden, limited pre-registration detail.
First large-scale causal test of celebrity influence on Twitter in a developing country; informs theory of diffusion and policy design for public health messaging.
Paper is clearly structured, thorough theoretical appendix, transparent about identification and caveats; tables/figures easy to follow.
Trial registered; but no public repository for data/code noted, Twitter data proprietary, limited replication materials, modest transparency beyond prereg.
Addresses vaccine promotion—global health priority—using scalable digital channels; findings informative for governments, NGOs worldwide on social-media strategy.
Combines solid theoretical advances with two carefully designed experiments and transparent replication files; limitations in external validity and reliance on artefactual settings temper impact.
Main claims are clearly stated and generally supported; heterogeneity analysis well aligned with theory, yet some estimates imprecise and assumptions (e.g. bias measurement) weaken strength.

Applies sufficient-statistic welfare framework, mixed-effects modelling, randomised experiments, and robustness checks; assumptions (normality, measurement error independence) plausible but not fully tested.
Provides first generalizable welfare criterion emphasizing distortion variance, likely to influence behavioural public-finance research; empirical illustration valuable though context-specific.
Well organised, clear derivations, intuitive examples, extensive appendices and visuals; minor density may challenge non-specialists.
Pre-registration, IRB approval, public registry, and posted replication files; data sharing depends on participant privacy, but documentation strong.
Findings inform policy debates on labels/taxes across many countries, yet experiments are US-centric and scenarios hypothetical, limiting immediate applicability to diverse contexts.
Large multi-country RCT, strong internal validity, high policy salience. Minor concerns on open data and some measurement limitations keep it from top decile.
Main claims (phone tutoring boosts learning, scalable via govt) align with evidence; effect sizes robust. Some extrapolations (dynamic complementarities, virtuous cycles) less directly tested.

Well-powered randomization, stratification, clustered SEs, multiple robustness checks, validity tests for phone assessment. Minor issues: unequal cluster levels, self-reported fidelity, limited pre-registration transparency.
First large experimental evidence on education-in-emergencies across five LMICs and govt delivery; informs scale literature and cost-effectiveness rankings.
Paper is comprehensive, clearly structured, transparent about limitations; sometimes verbose and dense, but arguments generally coherent and well supported.
Working paper shares extensive appendices, but datasets/code not yet publicly archived; preregistration not referenced; replication materials uncertain.
Addresses learning loss for low-resource contexts, aligns with SDG4 and humanitarian needs; highly actionable for policymakers worldwide.

Ambitious, well‐executed empirical study with large novel data and credible identification. Evidence is persuasive and writing clear, but limits remain (single-country setting, complex instruments, replication frictions) so not top-decile across all criteria.

Main claims are explicitly stated and supported with multiple consistency checks; IV strength high and extensive robustness shown. Some residual endogeneity worries (shift–share exposure, political instruments) keep it shy of very top.

Innovative construction of firm-specific exposure, sophisticated Bartik IV, deep-learning text similarity, rich fixed effects. Methods state-of-the-art for IO/innovation. Minor concerns about exclusion restriction and functional form.

Clarifies heterogeneous channels through which public science matters for incumbents, challenging common spillover narrative. Likely influential in innovation-policy literature, though limited to US public firms and basic productivity link.
Paper is long but logically structured; conceptual framework ties to empirics; diagrams and tables helpful. Some density and repetition impede accessibility for non-specialists.
Provides link to DISCERN dataset and describes construction, yet code not fully released and some proprietary sources (Dimensions, Compustat) impede full replication. No pre-registration.
Findings inform science-policy and R&D subsidy design, but analysis focused on US context and publicly listed firms; relevance to emerging economies or SMEs extrapolative.

Large administrative dataset, innovative RD-IV design, clear policy relevance; some uncertainty about generalizability and replication limits. Strength across categories yields solid upper-quartile quality.

Main claims (PEP boosts firm creation, magnitude, timing) are well-stated and backed by multiple estimators, placebo checks, heterogeneity; moderate risk remains from instrument validity and measurement error.
Creative running-variable instrument using rainfall plus extensive robustness, fixed effects, balance tests. Method carefully documented; some complexity and modeling choices could hide sensitivity.

Adds first causal evidence on legalization’s effect on entrepreneurship in developing context and introduces transferable methodology; contribution notable but niche to migration/entrepreneurship subfield.
Paper is long but arguments flow logically, visuals and tables support text, assumptions explicitly discussed; minor density and technicality may hinder non-specialists.
Uses confidential administrative data not publicly shareable; no public code repository referenced; robustness described but limited reproducibility for outsiders.
Addresses mass migration, legalization policy, and entrepreneurship in Global South; findings directly inform humanitarian and economic policy worldwide.
Innovative TVA method plus large RCT; strong methods and clear writing. Some uncertainty about external adoption and open-science practices keeps score below top decile.
Main claims (TVA consistency; best-policy effects) are supported by proofs, simulations, and applied RCT. Minor risk that assumptions (exact sparsity, beta-min) limit generality.

Careful design: Puffer-LASSO, winner’s-curse adjustment, large factorial RCT with proper clustering. Rigorous proofs and extensive simulations. Some reliance on homoskedasticity and oracle tuning remains.
Introduces practical framework for high-dimensional policy selection; could influence future experimental design. Field application yields actionable insights on immunization nudges.
Paper is well structured; assumptions and steps clearly laid out with diagrams and algorithms; lengthy but logically coherent. Dense math may limit accessibility to some practitioners.
Pre-analysis plan registered; code for TVA likely available in appendix but raw administrative data may be restricted; not all materials readily hosted in public repository.
Addresses childhood immunization uptake, a high-priority global health issue; method generalizable to other policy bundles; collaboration with government enhances impact.

Large, carefully executed RCT with prominent authors; strong methods, credible evidence and high policy relevance. Minor uncertainties on ultimate external validity and open-science completeness keep it shy of very top tier.
Main claims (economic expansion, labor re-allocation, mental-health effects) are clearly stated and supported by pre-registered analyses, multiple data sources and sensible robustness checks.

Cluster-RCT with 295 villages, transparent randomisation, high power, Conley SEs, pre-analysis plan, heterogeneity & attrition checks. Design admirably addresses spillovers and compliance; few papers reach this rigor.
First large-scale test of multi-year UBI with head-to-head comparison to alternative cash designs; offers new insight into lumpy investment & transfer design. Longer-run outcomes still pending.
Paper is long but well organised; theoretical model ties to empirics; tables & footnotes mostly clear. Some sections dense and could streamline exposition.
Pre-registered, codebook signals intention to share; GiveDirectly data proprietary but likely to be released after de-identification. Replication package not yet public at time of reading.
Addresses poverty alleviation and welfare-state design in LMICs; findings highly salient for governments, NGOs and donors considering cash transfers worldwide.

Solid modeling, clear exposition, and relevant policy insights put work above average, but heavy reliance on unverifiable assumptions, limited openness, and absence of peer review keep it shy of top tier.

Main claims (megafund not financially viable without public support) are supported by Monte-Carlo results, sensitivity checks, and comparison to prices, but evidence is entirely model-based; empirical validation lacking.

Uses reasonable Monte-Carlo framework, biologically motivated correlation matrix, and extensive sensitivity analyses. Yet parameter calibration is partly ad-hoc and no external validation or robustness to structural uncertainty.
Extends earlier megafund literature, quantifies mRNA‐specific issues, and informs policy debates; contribution is incremental rather than breakthrough.
Narrative is clear, assumptions stated, figures/tables helpful, and limitations acknowledged; logical flow largely sound.
No code or data released; model details are described but not enough for easy replication; working paper status without preregistration.
Addresses financing of vaccines for emerging infectious diseases, a critical global-health priority; findings directly inform governments and funders on pandemic preparedness.
Large, well-powered RCT with careful analysis and clear results; limitations on long-run follow-up and open-science lower the ceiling.
Main claims are specific and supported by sizable ITT effects, robustness checks, and heterogeneity analysis; short (2-3 month) horizon and self-reported outcomes introduce some uncertainty.

Stratified randomization, randomization-inference p-values, pre-specified indices, LASSO predictive heterogeneity—state-of-the-art for field RCTs; absence of pre-registration and attrition discussion slightly weaken confidence.
Demonstrates that lay-delivered group CBT can improve mental health and economic proxies in general poor population—fills gap beyond targeted therapy; long-term impact unknown.
Paper is generally well-structured with thorough tables and an ethics appendix, though length and dense discussion impair accessibility; some causal pathways arguments are speculative.
Detailed methods & ethics appendix provided; but code/data availability not yet indicated, and no formal pre-analysis plan referenced.
Addresses mental-health treatment gaps in low-income settings with scalable intervention; findings highly pertinent to LMIC policy and SDG3.

Ambitious theory–empirics paper by leading scholars; sound modelling, original field data, large cross-country tests. Some measurement and endogeneity concerns plus limited open-science practices temper the rating.
Clear claims; multiple data sets and robustness checks give credible support. Remaining doubts over causal identification and use of perceptions as proxies lower certainty.
Evolutionary model well crafted; empirical work uses PCA, OLS with rich controls, RI p-values. Yet limited causal strategies (no IV, RCT) and potential measurement error keep it below top decile.
Introduces novel concept of effort-suppressing beliefs, links zero-sum perceptions to growth; likely to open new research avenues in cultural economics and development.
Paper is long but extremely clear; theoretical and empirical sections well connected; transparent derivations; extensive robustness tables.
Working paper publicly available; appendices give proofs and some data description, but raw data, code and pre-analysis are not yet fully shared; no replication package online.
Addresses development outcomes across low- and high-income contexts; field data from DRC plus global WVS make findings broadly pertinent to policy and academia.

Synthesises replication literature to guide CEA discounts; clear and useful but largely heuristic, with limited original analysis and modest transparency. Solid communication and relevance raise score, but methodological rigor and open-science practices constrain it.

Main claims (need for separate internal/external validity discounts and size heuristics) align with cited literature. Evidence is secondary and selectively drawn; not a systematic review, but citations are current and appropriate. Confidence intervals and robustness checks are absent.

Approach is narrative review plus rule-of-thumb derivation; transparent but informal. No formal search strategy, bias assessment or reproducible calculations. Relies on back-of-envelope power heuristics; useful yet below median methodological rigor for recent meta-research.

Provides actionable framework for cost-effectiveness analysts, filling a practical gap between academic meta-research and philanthropic decision making. Contribution is chiefly integrative rather than novel; impact highest within EA/CEA niche, moderate for broader replicability field.

Well-structured, with clear definitions, step-by-step guidance, illustrative examples and concise summaries. Arguments generally coherent. Minor redundancies and reliance on jargon without full formal derivations prevent higher score.

Cites sources and includes appendix, but no shared code, data, or systematic protocol; spreadsheets referenced are not fully public. No preregistration. Transparency adequate for narrative piece but below field best practice.

Targets global health & development interventions and philanthropic resource allocation. Guidance could materially influence funding effectiveness worldwide. Applicability limited outside RCT-heavy evaluation contexts, but still above average on practical importance.

Well-designed RCT follow-up, clear writing, substantial policy value and solid statistical practice place the work in the top quintile of recent development-econ / global-mental-health papers. Some uncertainty stems from limited economic impacts and data/code availability.
Main claims are narrow, quantitatively stated, and backed by preregistered ITT analyses, multiple robustness checks, expert-prediction benchmark, and clear reporting of limitations.

Use of two original RCTs with 4–5-year follow-up, double-ML adjustment, multiple-hypothesis correction, mediation and heterogeneity analyses is advanced and transparent. Remaining risk: attrition (24 %), self-reported outcomes.
Provides rare long-run evidence on psychotherapy in LMICs and novel behavioural measures. Moves expert beliefs and cost-effectiveness estimates. Economic nulls limit transformative impact.
Storyline and figures are clear; assumptions and statistical choices explained; supplementary material thorough. Length and density may challenge non-specialists.
Trials preregistered; replication appendix promised; references to public registry numbers given. At time of working paper, full code and anonymised data not yet posted.
Targets mental health in low-income settings, uses scalable lay-counsellor model, and yields cost-effectiveness estimates salient for LMIC health policy and donors.
Conceptual essay with clear narrative but limited empirical backing or new data resources. Quality averages out: strong exposition yet modest methodological rigor and open-science practice.
Plausible claims that citation incentives steer research; supporting evidence mainly anecdotal, literature-based, and correlational. No causal tests, leaving credibility moderate–low.
Relies on simple illustrative model and secondary bibliometric analyses. Appropriate for agenda-setting but limited rigor, robustness checks, or alternative explanations.
Introduces ‘edge factor’ concept and incentive framing that has influenced discourse on scientific stagnation. Adds some novel direction though incremental relative to existing bibliometrics work.
Argument is clearly structured, concepts defined, rich historical examples, minimal logical leaps. Some over-statement of causality lowers ceiling.
No new dataset or code released; analyses not fully reproducible. Uses publicly available PubMed data but without shared processing pipeline.
Addresses worldwide slowdown in productivity and proposes broadly applicable policy reforms. Applicability high, though evidence US-centric and abstract.
Careful empirical work, large novel finding, solid modelling. Some remaining identification uncertainty and heavy macro assumptions prevent top-decile placement.
Clearly stated claims; many robustness checks; still correlational time-series evidence and disputable structural mapping keep confidence below top tier.
Appropriate Hamilton filter, local projections, model inversion. Methodological craft strong, but small sample, linearity, and reliance on assumed damage function add risk.
Shifts benchmark SCC by an order of magnitude, challenges prevailing panel literature, offers new top-down approach—high incremental contribution.
Narrative is well-structured, derivations transparent, extensive appendix; minor complexity may impede some readers.
Data sources public, but code/materials not yet released; replication feasible but not turnkey.
Addresses worldwide climate damages, SCC, policy costs, directly pertinent to global priorities and large economies.
Solid RCT with clear policy relevance and competent analysis, but moderate sample size, reliance on self-reported financial outcomes, and limited open-science practices keep it from the top tier.

Main ITT effects are credibly estimated and interpretation mostly careful; however, key secondary outcomes (tax revenue, revenue growth) rest on sparse or self-reported data and mechanism evidence is exploratory, reducing certainty.

Randomization, balance checks, ANCOVA, and IV analyses are appropriate; attrition minimal. Yet no pre-registration, modest power, potential reporting bias in revenue/tax receipts, and limited robustness checks temper confidence.

First field RCT on civic-information interventions for informal-sector taxation; surprising negative extensive-margin effect stimulates new theory and policy debate, likely to influence subsequent work in public-finance development.

Paper is well structured, theoretical framework aligns with findings, discussion of alternative explanations provided; some sections lengthy and exploratory analyses sometimes blur preregistered vs post-hoc.
No mention of pre-analysis plan, public code, or data availability; modest description of materials. Some implementation details supplied, but replication not readily possible.
Addresses tax capacity in low-income countries, a central development priority; findings immediately relevant for fiscal authorities and donors working on informal-sector integration.

Exploratory study presents novel animal-welfare cost estimates but relies on small, hypothetical survey with acknowledged biases; communication good but methodological and evidence weaknesses pull quality to modest level.

Main claims (animal lives not worth living; welfare costs exceed benefits) exceed strength of evidence, which is based on stated preferences subject to large hypothetical and sampling bias; authors candidly discuss limits but inference still weak.

Uses standard contingent-valuation with WTP/WTA, but sample (N≈300 after exclusions), heavy non-response, extreme skew, ad-hoc trimming, limited robustness checks; minimal preregistration or bias-mitigation; hence below-average rigor.
Adds first-order quantitative figures for animal-welfare externalities and links to tax policy; novelty for welfare economics, yet precision low and context narrow, so moderate contribution.

Paper logically structures theory, survey, results, candid limitations; math and tables clear, citations thorough. Some long exposition and complex framing but overall reasoning transparent and coherent.
No public data, code, or preregistration reported; survey instrument partly described but replication difficult; thus below current field norms.
Animal-welfare impacts of meat and tax design are globally pertinent, yet study uses Belgian sample and hypothetical scenarios limiting external validity; relevance average.

Large-scale, well-designed nationwide RCT on environmental governance; strong empirical execution, clear writing, and important policy implications. Minor limits: working-paper status, modest open-science practices.

Main claims (public vs private appeals effects; regulator incentives) are explicitly stated and supported by multiple experimental contrasts, robustness and heterogeneity checks. Some secondary mechanism tests are suggestive rather than conclusive.

Sophisticated multi-level randomisation, credible identification, appropriate fixed-effects, clustering, pre-analysis clarity, GE design. Possible concerns: shortened study horizon, potential spill-ins unmeasured, limited pre-registration details.

First large RCT on citizen participation & environmental enforcement in China; documents sizeable effects and GE non-offsets, informing theory of authoritarian accountability and environmental policy.
Paper is clearly structured, motivates hypotheses, explains context, presents results with intuitive figures/tables; reasoning transparent, limitations acknowledged.
Data appendix available; uses administrative data. Code availability not explicit, limited pre-registration detail; working paper but not full replication package yet.
Findings on low-cost citizen engagement, social media, and regulatory behavior have clear relevance for LMIC environmental governance and global pollution reduction priorities.
Solid experimental study with clear analysis and policy relevance; limits include modest response rate, hypothetical choices, and field-specific scope, so impact and certainty are moderate.

Main claims (scientists value dissensus) are supported by well-powered discrete-choice data, robustness checks, and re-analysis of external datasets, but reliance on stated preferences introduces external-validity concerns.

Experimental design, randomization, conditional‐ and multinomial-logit estimation, and heterogeneity analysis are appropriate and transparent; however, potential non-response bias and hypothetical context limit methodological strength.
Provides new quantitative evidence relevant to reforming grant peer review and risk-taking; contribution is timely but incremental, and real-world behavioral effects remain to be demonstrated.
Paper is well organized, with clear motivation, transparent reasoning, thorough robustness checks, and readable presentation; minor length and complexity may hinder some audiences.
Data appendix and detailed materials are publicly linked; methods, code description, and questionnaire excerpts enable replication, though full raw data/code not yet in an open repository.
Findings most directly affect US biomedical funding but principles generalize to global science agencies; policy implications are discussed yet not tailored to diverse funding environments.

Solid, preregistered multi-study paper linking moral psychology and population ethics; strong methods and transparency give it an edge, but reliance on MTurk samples and hypothetical vignettes curb ceiling performance.

Main claims (asymmetry in valuing happiness/suffering; mixed average vs. total welfare intuitions; effect of reflection) are generally supported by nine adequately powered studies, but evidence is limited to self-report judgments in artificial tasks.

Large preregistered online samples, attention checks, power analyses, multiple robustness checks, and clear stats. Limitations: convenience sampling, hypothetical scenarios, some exclusion rates high, limited cross-culturally.

First comprehensive empirical look at population-ethical intuitions; opens new dialogue between psychology and philosophy, but findings are incremental for psychology and speculative for normative theory.
Paper is well-structured, arguments explicit, limitations discussed, visuals clear, connects results to theory; minor verbosity and some speculative leaps prevent top score.
All materials, data, code, preregistrations openly provided on OSF; disclosure of exclusions and power; exemplary transparency for the field.
Implications for long-term policy and existential risk are noted but indirect; results stem from WEIRD samples and hypothetical judgments, limiting immediate applicability to global decision-making.

Careful comparison of epidemiological and reduced-form approaches, solid empirical work and clear exposition. Limited primarily by moderate methodological innovation and by being a working paper without peer-review or open materials.

Main claims are clearly articulated and supported with multiple robustness checks and sensitivity analyses; however, evidence that disease severity drives long-run effects is suggestive rather than definitive.

Combines dynamic SIR accounting with difference-in-difference style regressions. Implementation appears competent and validated, yet relies on strong assumptions (uniform infection risk, reporting-rate estimation) and uses aggregate data with potential ecological bias.
Adds a useful head-to-head test of two common empirical paradigms and offers policy-relevant insight, but does not overturn existing consensus or provide fundamentally new theory.
Well-structured, transparent reasoning, comprehensive figures and tables, limitations discussed. Minor density and rotation of some graphics slightly impede readability.
Uses entirely public data sources; however, no code archive or replication package is referenced, and reporting-rate estimation details would benefit from shared scripts.
Findings inform vaccine-impact valuation, especially for LMIC settings with high measles burden, but empirical context is historical US; direct applicability to current global policy is indirect.

Ambitious integrative modelling of science returns vs bio-risk with transparent assumptions. Solid reasoning but relies on many speculative parameters and limited validation; open-science practices moderate. Overall quality modest-to-good.

Key claims clearly stated and tied to quantitative models; draws on XPT forecasts and literature. Evidence base for several critical parameters (health impact, extinction utility) remains thin and partly subjective.
Combines semi-endogenous growth, DALY valuation, and probabilistic risk; math correct, but heavy simplifying assumptions, limited sensitivity to structural uncertainty, no empirical validation.
First systematic ROI estimate of ‘science vs tech-risk’ dilemma; offers novel framework useful for policy debate and future work despite parameter fragility.
Well-structured, transparent derivations, clear tables; plentiful caveats. Lengthy exposition occasionally obscures key points but logical flow mostly sound.
Paper shares detailed appendices and spreadsheets; code referenced but not fully released or documented; relies on proprietary forecast dataset; reproducibility moderate.
Addresses worldwide welfare, pandemics, science funding; insights pertinent to philanthropy and policy. Applicability limited by high-income assumptions and speculative long-term focus.

Well-executed systematic review/meta-analysis with credible methods, clear exposition and strong policy salience. Limitations stem from exclusive reliance on observational studies, residual confounding and moderate openness of materials. Quality sits comfortably in the upper third of recent work but is not field-leading.

Central claims are clearly stated and supported by comprehensive literature search, duplicate extraction, publication-bias checks and sensitivity analyses. Evidence strength limited by non-experimental primary studies; authors acknowledge this and perform robustness assessments, so credibility remains high.

Applies current best-practice meta-analytic tools (robust variance, PET-PEESE, Oster bounds, specification curve). Search strategy and inclusion criteria transparent. Some subjective choices (re-expression algorithm, covariate adjustments) and lack of preregistration keep score below top decile.

Extends prior IQ-focused reviews to learning outcomes and LMIC policy simulations, offering useful quantitative benchmarks. Novelty moderate; insights incremental rather than transformative, but still valuable for education and public-health prioritisation.
Structure logical, assumptions explicit, figures/tables aid understanding, limitations candidly discussed. Writing accessible to multidisciplinary audiences, including policymakers.
Working paper is freely available; search strings and study list provided. However, raw extraction sheets and analysis code are not fully deposited in a public repository, limiting easy reproduction.

Addresses widespread lead exposure affecting hundreds of millions of children in LMICs, links to education outcomes, and evaluates cost-effective interventions—high practical importance for global health and development priorities.

Solid, well-argued paper that opens a new line of cost-effectiveness work for food-system resilience, but relies on speculative inputs and small expert survey; quality sits moderately above field median.
Main claims are clearly stated and sensitivity tests run, yet empirical grounding is weak (n=8 survey, many unverifiable priors), so evidential strength is below average.
Monte-Carlo framework is standard and transparently described; however parameter elicitation, independence assumptions, and model structure have notable shortcomings, limiting robustness.
First quantitative comparison of resilient foods vs AGI safety; stimulates debate and follow-on work, providing useful starting point despite uncertainty.
Paper is well organised, lays out assumptions, includes extensive discussion of uncertainty; some sections verbose and technical, but reasoning mostly transparent and consistent.
Guesstimate and Analytica models publicly shared, parameters documented, encourages readers to modify; good reproducibility for policy modelling literature.
Addresses globally significant risks (nuclear winter, AI), emphasizes cost-effective interventions applicable worldwide; high salience for policymakers and philanthropy.
Carefully designed lab-field experiment with credible identification, clear writing, preregistration, and useful insights; sample limits and short-lived effects temper impact.
Main claims clearly stated and supported by randomized encouragement and IPW; replication in field strengthens evidence though modest sample and attrition windows add some uncertainty.
Design leverages random price draw and preregistration; statistical analysis appropriate; some reliance on self-reported WTP and limited power due to COVID reduce robustness.
Extends willful-ignorance literature to real consumption with VR intervention; novel cost-effectiveness discussion; context narrow and effects fade quickly, so contribution moderate.
Paper well structured, transparent, thorough appendices, clear linkage of theory and results; minor complexity may challenge non-specialists.
Pre-registered, IRB approved, appendices detailed; registry ID provided. Data/code availability not yet public in text; hence moderate.
Meat consumption and climate/animal welfare globally important; yet sample is German students and intervention costly (VR), limiting immediate policy applicability.
Strong RCT-based evidence with clear exposition and high global relevance; some limitations in open-science and external validity temper the overall standing.
Main claims (efficiency & health impacts of bundled incentives) are clearly stated and tightly linked to the presented evidence; robustness and heterogeneity checks increase credibility.
Random assignment, DiD, event-study, bootstrapping, and balance tests are appropriate; some residual threats (spillovers, attrition, partial data) acknowledged but not fully ruled out.
Adds rare causal evidence on nonprofit governance in low-income settings and highlights complementarity of financing and monitoring; novelty moderate for RCT literature but impactful for policy.
Well-structured, lucid writing, clear tables/figures, motivates theory and interprets results carefully; minor length/complexity issues for non-specialists.
Data appendix and detailed description provided, but raw data are not publicly posted and replication code unavailable at time of review.
Targets maternal/infant health in DRC—a critical SDG area; findings readily inform donors, NGOs, and governments across LMICs.
Solid theoretical framing and clear empirical illustration place it modestly above median recent work, but limited originality and modest empirical rigor keep it from the top tier.
Main claims are supported by descriptive statistics and simple regressions; evidence is relevant but not especially strong or causal, leaving some claims only suggestively backed.
Uses standard public-goods theory and basic OLS on secondary data. Assumptions (uniform MC, price indices as proxies) are debatable and robustness limited, yielding average methodological strength.
Extends public-goods lens to pharma pricing and quantifies country contributions, offering useful perspective though not a major breakthrough.
Argument is clearly structured, theoretical sections well connected to empirics, writing lucid, figures and tables intelligible; minor verbosity but reasoning mostly transparent.
Relies on publicly available RAND and PWT data but no shared code, limited replication materials, and no preregistration; transparency moderate to low.
Addresses international drug pricing, free-riding and R&D incentives—issues important for global health and policy; findings have potential policy utility across countries.

Well-executed, novel study linking biodiversity risk to asset prices by constructing aggregate news indices and firm exposure measures. Strong authorship, clear writing, solid validation, and public data release place it in top quintile, though still a working paper with some open robustness questions.

Main claims (new indices, heterogeneous exposures, partial pricing) are supported by multiple converging evidence sources (text mining, survey, portfolio tests). Some reliance on sentiment models and AR(1) surprises may be questioned, hence slight uncertainty.

Uses state-of-the-art NLP (BERT), survey, hedge-portfolio regressions, multiple-testing control. Assumptions (keyword lists, sentiment sign) reasonable but not bullet-proof; modest sensitivity analyses; preregistration absent.

First systematic quantification of biodiversity financial risk; widely cited potential; releases exposure data to spur follow-up. Distinct from climate finance literature, thus high incremental contribution.
Paper is logically structured, arguments transparent, visuals clear, limitations acknowledged, comparison with climate risk carefully laid out.
Authors publicly release exposure datasets and provide dictionary; working paper references GitHub site, but full code and raw survey microdata not yet fully available; no preregistration.
Biodiversity loss is a pressing global priority; results applicable across industries and countries; focus on U.S. data tempers applicability somewhat but relevance remains high.
Solid methodology and transparency yield high marks, but limited number of eligible RCTs and modest novelty temper impact.
Main claims are clearly stated and supported by appropriate meta-analytic evidence; some inferences (e.g., substitution effects) remain speculative.
Uses preregistered inclusion criteria, robust variance meta-analysis, multiple publication-bias checks, and reproducible code; residual risk from single-coder extraction and unsystematic search.
Provides the most rigorous synthesis to date, challenges optimistic prior reviews, but actionable guidance is limited given small pooled effects and heterogeneity.
Narrative is well structured; figures/tables aid understanding; some lengthy digressions and dense citations slightly hinder uptake by non-specialists.
Code, data, and containerized workflow publicly archived; clear documentation; only moderate risk-of-bias coding missing a second reviewer.
Findings bear directly on climate, health, and animal-welfare priorities worldwide, especially for policy makers exploring demand-side mitigation options.

Ambitious synthesis of 96 rigorously-evaluated climate policies, coherent use of MVPF, novel learning-by-doing treatment, transparent assumptions. Minor concerns on heterogeneity handling and reliance on SCC choices prevent top-decile score.

Research questions clear; draws on credible quasi-/experimental literature; evidence well summarized. Some elasticity extrapolations and publication-bias corrections are coarse, giving modest uncertainty.

Sound welfare-economics framework with innovative sufficient-statistics for spillovers; careful harmonisation of externalities. Limitations: strong pass-through/full-competition assumptions, limited sensitivity to alternative demand specs.
Provides first large-scale, comparable MVPF estimates for climate policies; clarifies subsidy/tax trade-offs; likely to inform policy design and future research agendas.
Paper is long but remarkably clear; assumptions and computations laid out, extensive appendices and visuals facilitate comprehension; logical flow solid.
Authors state all code and data on GitHub and rely on public sources; replication seems feasible. Some proprietary datasets (Opower) not fully open.
Findings directly inform climate-policy cost-effectiveness across sectors; includes international cases and incidence discussion, though US-centric baseline limits universality.

Large, preregistered RCT with clear reporting and policy-relevant topic. Execution and communication strong; minor limitations (single country, one-year horizon, some interpretive leaps) temper top-tier status.

Main claims (cash improves econ & mental health; PM+ does not) are directly tested with adequate power, multiple robustness checks and conservative p-adjustments. Interpretation of nulls carefully discussed, though causal mechanisms less explored.

Well-designed cluster-RCT; pre-analysis plan; ANCOVA; multiple-hypothesis FDR; heterogeneity & spillover analyses; demand-effect test. Minor concerns: some post-hoc exploratory work, possible implementation fidelity issues.

Adds credible comparative evidence on cash vs psychotherapy in LMICs; informs cost-effectiveness debate. However, findings align with earlier cash-transfer literature and external validity beyond setting/specification remains to be shown.
Paper is well-structured, transparent, with detailed appendix and clear exposition of assumptions, stats and limitations. Lengthy discussion may obscure key takeaways for some audiences.

Pre-registered on AEA registry; materials and online appendix public. Data/code availability not fully open at time of working paper, though promised. Reasonably good but not exemplary compared with best-practice repositories.
Targets poverty, mental health, IPV in rural Kenya—issues central to SDGs and global development funding. Results inform cost-effective policy for LMICs and humanitarian actors.

Large-scale, methodologically careful study from leading scholars; robust analyses and policy-relevant insights. Some uncertainty from limits on open data/code and field-specific caveats, but overall among the stronger contributions in science-of-science research.
Main claims (existence, magnitude, and growth of pivot penalty) are clearly stated and supported by massive datasets, multiple robustness checks, natural experiments, and alternative outcomes.

Employs sensible cosine pivot metric, appropriate normalization, fixed-effects panels, DiD, IV; extensive robustness. Minor concerns over name-disambiguation, reliance on citation metrics, and limited discussion of causal assumptions.

Introduces generalizable ‘pivot penalty’ concept, quantifies adaptability limits across science & technology, and informs creativity/expertise debates; likely to shape future work and policy discussions.
Argument flows logically; figures and tables clear; limitations and alternative explanations discussed; writing highly accessible for multiple audiences.
Uses proprietary Dimensions and PatentsView data; supplementary materials detailed but no explicit code or full data release, limiting replicability.
Findings on research adaptability impact funding, crisis response, innovation policy worldwide; COVID-19 case heightens practical relevance across regions and disciplines.
Well-designed RCT addressing major environmental externality; strong empirical execution and clear writing. Slightly limited by modest novelty in PES literature and moderate openness of materials.
Main claims stated clearly and supported by multiple concordant outcome measures (monitoring, remote sensing, survey). Effect sizes and uncertainty reported; alternative explanations probed.

Cluster-RCT with pre-analysis plan, power considerations, balance tests, multiple robustness checks; innovative high-resolution ML fire detection. Minor concerns on potential training-set leakage and generalisability.
Adds credible evidence on contract design (up-front vs back-loaded) for PES in LMICs and on crop-burning mitigation; important but incremental within broader PES and air-pollution fields.
Argument flow is transparent, assumptions explicit, tables/figures clear, policy implications cautiously drawn; manuscript highly readable.
Pre-registered and reports trial registry; however, code, satellite‐classification model weights, and de-identified data not yet publicly posted, limiting full reproducibility.
Targets severe air-quality problem affecting hundreds of millions; findings generalisable to other crop-burning contexts and inform cost-effective abatement policies for LMICs.

Large preregistered RCT with >5k low-income US adults; transparent design, rich admin data, extensive robustness & mechanism work. Execution and reporting are first-rate, yet contribution partly limited by null/negative findings and U.S-specific scope.

Main claims (no positive effects of $500 or $2,000 UCTs; mechanism via salience) are clearly stated, tightly linked to preregistered analyses, and supported by survey, bank, and experimental evidence. Minor residual uncertainty from attrition and self-report bias keeps score below 85.

Randomized amounts, large sample, preregistration, multiple hypothesis correction, administrative validation, mediation tests, bounding and imputation for attrition—state of the art. Remaining weaknesses: 17% full attrition, self-selection into bank data, short follow-up.

Provides rare high-income-country evidence and challenges optimistic priors on cash transfers; includes expert-forecast component and theory contribution. Impact meaningful but not paradigm-shifting; external validity to other contexts and longer horizons remains open.

Writing is clear, structure logical, graphics and appendices comprehensive; reasoning transparent with limitations discussed. Dense 100+ page appendix may tax readers, but overall exposition exemplary.

AEARCTR preregistration, pre-analysis plan, detailed appendices, shared survey materials and code links; bank data cannot be fully public for privacy but procedures documented. Good but not perfect openness.

Findings inform design of cash programs in high-income settings and contribute to general debates on poverty and mental health. Direct applicability to global South or humanitarian contexts limited; amounts small relative to LMIC transfers.
Short AEA P&P piece: clear and policy-relevant but largely syntheses of prior work; limited new evidence or methodological depth. Balanced average of category scores seems appropriate.
States claims clearly and cites supporting figures, but relies on secondary sources and simple comparisons; no rigorous causal identification.
Presents stylized theoretical insights and descriptive comparisons; lacks detailed modeling or empirical strategy within the published piece.
Consolidates lessons from first AMC and highlights design trade-offs; incremental conceptual contribution, important but not groundbreaking.
Argument flow is logical, concise, and accessible; assumptions and limitations are acknowledged within tight space constraints.
Cites public data sources and working paper, but provides no new data or code; replication materials not necessary yet not supplied.
Addresses vaccine access for low-income countries and design of funding mechanisms; highly pertinent to global health policy and development priorities.

Rigorous systematic review & Bayesian/frequentist meta-analysis, clear policy-oriented cost‐effectiveness. Transparent, open code. Minor concerns: still moderate power, some reliance on author-provided data, and limited exploration of age-specific effects.

Main claims (≈25% U5 mortality reduction; high cost-effectiveness) are supported by systematic search, 18 RCTs, sensitivity & publication-bias checks. Evidence strong but limited by missing mortality data in many RCTs and residual heterogeneity.

Appropriate Bayesian & frequentist random-effects models, cluster corrections, extensive sensitivity analyses, cost-effectiveness modelling. Minor issues: assumptions on compliance, DALYs, linear extrapolations; power to detect moderators low.

Provides first quantitatively credible estimate of water-treatment impact on child mortality and links to economic value, likely to shift funding priorities. Less novel methodologically; incremental on prior diarrhea meta-analyses.
Well-structured, thorough explanation of search, modelling, sensitivity, limitations. Some density (97 pages) but argument remains traceable; graphs and tables aid clarity.
Pre-registered, PRISMA compliance, code & data on GitHub, author contact to obtain unpublished data, clear disclosure statements. Minor reliance on non-public cost data from NGO.
Addresses under-5 mortality in LMICs; evaluates scalable, low-cost interventions; provides region-specific cost-effectiveness helping donors/governments. Directly informs SDG-6 and SDG-3 priorities.
Solid causal-policy evaluation with good methods, robustness, open data/code, and clear writing. Limitations in external validity and some data‐quality issues keep it from top decile.
Claims are well stated; causal estimates supported with SDID, sensitivity and placebo tests. Evidence limited to one platform and potential misclassification, so moderate uncertainty.
Choice of SDID appropriate; seasonal controls, announcement exclusion, robustness checks strong. Weaknesses: reliance on NLP species ID, unobserved demand shocks, substitution criteria ad-hoc.
First rigorous evidence of spillovers from wildlife trade bans, informing conservation policy and economic theory of substitution; likely to spur further work.
Questions, assumptions, and results clearly laid out; figures/tables aid comprehension; argument flows logically. Minor jargon and lengthy SI may hinder some readers.
Authors promise public release of full data and R code; methods reproducible. Data scraped from public site may face future access limits and some raw steps manual.
Wildlife trade is a global priority; study offers actionable insights. Yet empirical focus is Japan and three taxa, so direct applicability to other regions/species is moderate.

Large, multi-decade dataset and two credible quasi-experiments yield policy-relevant causal estimates of GDP effects on biodiversity. Analyses are careful and transparent, but US-only scope, representativeness limits, and some weaker first stages in subsamples temper impact and certainty.
Clear questions, extensive robustness, two independent IV strategies, and channel decomposition support main claims. Remaining external-validity and sampling-bias caveats acknowledged but unresolved.
Appropriate panel FE, shift-share and wind IVs, LASSO instrument, multiple diagnostics. Sound but some instruments weak in full sample; measurement error and non-random site coverage remain.

First broad causal estimates linking economic activity, pollution, and biodiversity across taxa; informs environmental-economic accounting. Contribution somewhat bounded by US focus and dataset coverage.
Argument flow is logical; assumptions mostly explicit; numerous figures and tables aid interpretation. Long paper with dense appendices may challenge non-specialists.
Relies on publicly available BioTIME and standard economic data; methods detailed. However, code availability not stated and some processed data steps may limit full reproducibility.
Findings on economic growth–biodiversity trade-offs and regulation co-benefits are relevant to global policy debates, but empirical evidence is US-centric and ecosystem coverage uneven.

In-depth, transparent cost-effectiveness evaluation linking psychotherapy to WELLBYs; combines large systematic review with charity data. Some methodological novelty and open materials, but remaining uncertainties on spillovers, dosage, and weighting temper top-tier ranking.

Main claims (5-6× cash transfers) are clearly stated and generally supported by extensive meta-analysis, RCTs and M&E data. Authors openly discuss caveats, yet rely on limited spillover evidence and subjective weighting, leaving some claims less securely grounded.

Applies rigorous systematic review (84 RCTs), multilevel meta-regressions, time-decay modelling, bias adjustments, Monte-Carlo CIs. Creative but defensible weighting scheme; code shared. However, synthetic controls for pre-post and several ad-hoc adjustments introduce methodological fragility.

First comprehensive WELLBY cost-effectiveness estimates for psychotherapy charities in LMICs; offers transferable framework and highlights evidence gaps (spillovers, attendance). Advances practical prioritisation, but insights are incremental within global mental‐health economics.

Report is lengthy but well-structured, definitions clear, assumptions explicit, robustness checks extensive, figures/tables aid comprehension. Minor density and occasional complexity may hinder non-specialists.

Protocol preregistered; full report, spreadsheets, and R code promised; systematic review data shared. Raw charity data understandably restricted, and some weighting judgements not reproducible, slightly limiting full reproducibility.

Addresses neglected burden of depression/anxiety in sub-Saharan Africa; compares to cash benchmark to guide donors; findings directly inform philanthropic and policy allocations toward cost-effective mental-health interventions.
Large-scale RCT on international migration with careful analysis, but some attrition and open-science limits keep it below very top tier.
Main questions clearly stated; strong first-stage; multiple data sources; effect sizes convincing. Some reliance on assumptions for MTE and wellbeing valuation.
Random assignment within recruiter pools, appropriate FE & clustering, IV, bounding. Attrition handled but still imbalanced; linear MTE extrapolation debatable.
Fills major gap on guest-worker programs, measures pecuniary & non-pecuniary costs, informs policy. Novel reservation wage & broker fee data.
Well-structured, transparent derivations, rich tables/figures; clearly discusses limitations.
AEARCTR preregistration noted; working paper publicly available. Code/data availability not yet evident; some admin data restricted.
Addresses massive South Asia–Gulf migration corridor; results directly inform labor, migration, development policy globally.

Solid, innovative spatial-GE model and policy-relevant results; evidence credible but calibrated; openness and robustness moderate. Overall quality around upper-middle of recent environmental-econ research.

Main claims (limited leakage, effectiveness of Brazilian policies) stated clearly and supported by model-based counterfactuals plus reduced-form checks. However, heavy reliance on calibrated parameters and some pre-trend concerns temper evidential strength.

Combines rich spatial GE, migration, trade, and deforestation supply with careful calibration and gravity / migration estimations. Techniques at frontier though many assumptions, limited sensitivity analysis, and no formal estimation of all parameters.

Introduces general-equilibrium lens to leakage debate, quantifies policy impacts over time, and integrates land-use, trade, and migration—valuable contribution but incremental relative to emerging spatial-economics literature.

Argument flows logically; equations, figures, and empirical context well documented. Draft still long and occasionally dense; some sections (e.g., data construction) could be clearer, yet overall communication above average.
Uses fully public datasets and describes processing, but no code or replication package provided, model inversion details partly opaque. Pre-registration and robustness archives absent.

Deforestation, climate mitigation, and land-use policy are global priorities. Results directly inform design of conservation strategies and international finance mechanisms; insights transferable to other forest frontiers.

Solid, transparent survey offering novel empirical input to AGI-safety governance. Credibility somewhat limited by small, non-random sample and Western-centric expert pool, but methods are competent and reporting clear. Contribution is meaningful yet not field-defining.

Main claim—broad expert agreement on 50 practices—is well supported by descriptive statistics. However, purposive sampling, modest N (51) and possible social-desirability bias temper strength. Authors accurately discuss limitations.

Standard survey design and Likert analysis; pre-registered; Mann-Whitney & chi-square tests. Non-probability sampling and limited statistical power reduce rigor. Overall adequate for exploratory aims but not cutting-edge.

First systematic mapping of expert consensus on AGI lab best practices; useful for policymakers, standards bodies, and future research agendas. Still early-stage; findings need broader, more diverse replication.

Paper is well structured, defines terms, states questions, explains analysis, and contextualizes results. Figures and tables are clear; discussion thoughtfully links evidence to claims and policy implications.

Survey instrument, pre-registration, code, and anonymized data shared on OSF; deviations from plan documented. Full raw data withheld for privacy, but transparency otherwise high relative to field norms.

AGI safety practices impact global risk; results pertinent to EU, US, UK regulation. Expert pool and framing mainly Western, limiting inclusivity, yet content broadly applicable to international governance efforts.
Solid theoretical advance with clear models and proofs; some simplifying assumptions and lack of empirical validation temper impact. Overall quality above recent‐years median for econ/x-risk papers.
Main claims are logically derived and internally consistent; evidence is purely theoretical, no empirical calibration or robustness tests, so strength moderate.
Uses formal dynamic optimization, hazard integration, and comparative statics rigorously; proofs sound. Assumptions stylized, limited sensitivity analysis.
Introduces state vs. transition risk trade-off and ER Kuznets curve, clarifying policy implications; likely to shape future growth/x-risk research.
Paper well organized, definitions clear, proofs detailed; writing dense but follows economic theory norms.
Appendix provides replication code for simulations and full proofs, but no public repository for LaTeX/source; models not in executable notebook; adequate but not exemplary.
Addresses existential risk trade-offs central to global priorities; insights useful for policymakers and AI/climate governance discussions.

Well-executed RCT with 23-year follow-up, novel intergenerational mortality finding, solid communication. Some limits (self-reported child deaths, partial mechanism identification, data-sharing constraints) keep it below very top tier.
Main claim (22 % U5MR reduction) tightly linked to random assignment, multiple robustness checks. Infant-mortality effect nonsignificant and mechanisms not causally pinned, tempering confidence.

Uses original RCT, appropriate LPM/logit, clustering, weighting, attrition analysis, dose-response. Minor concerns: recall of child deaths, multiple testing adjustment thin, complex weighting choices.
Provides rare causal evidence of intergenerational health gains in LMICs; informs cost-effectiveness debate on deworming and broader human-capital policy.
Clear narrative, transparent assumptions, helpful figures. Paper lengthy; some sections (cost-benefit, mediation) densely presented, but reasoning generally easy to follow.
Pre-registered on AEA and extensive appendices. Code availability unclear; KLPS data partly restricted. Replication possible with access, but not fully turnkey.
Addresses child mortality in LICs, policy-salient intervention recommended by WHO; cost-benefit analysis aids donors and governments worldwide.
High‐profile study with solid methods, strong evidence, clear writing, major global relevance. Some modelling limitations and partial code availability temper a perfect score.

Main claims (spatial extent, carbon potential) are clearly stated and backed by large‐sample remote‐sensing analysis with extensive validation (≈88% accuracy). Still relies on assumptions about future persistence and excludes belowground carbon, so evidence not definitive.

State-of-the-art 30 m random-forest modelling, thoughtful variable selection, autocorrelation checks, sensitivity analysis. Limitations: mixed-resolution predictors, observational design, modest handling of socioeconomic dynamics.
Provides first high-resolution pantropical map of natural regeneration potential, actionable for restoration targets and carbon markets; likely to shape policy and research agendas.
Narrative is concise, well-structured, assumptions explicit, visuals clear. Conclusions generally align with results; caveats discussed.
Key raster outputs on Zenodo; uses public datasets. Full analysis code only ‘available on request’, limiting reproducibility. Some very large files may hinder access.
Addresses tropical restoration, carbon sequestration, biodiversity—central to climate and SDG agendas; identifies priority countries, directly informs practitioners and policymakers worldwide.
Large‐scale, well-executed quasi-experimental study that links urban greening to pollution and health. Some endogeneity concerns and limited data/code transparency temper top scores.
Main claims (pollution ↓, pollen ↑, health mix) are clearly stated and supported with multiple data sources and robustness checks, yet causal chain relies on several modelling assumptions.

Combines remote sensing, wind-based panel IV, and claims data; addresses interference creatively. Remaining risks: digitised polygons accuracy, short time windows, limited IV strength for health stage.
Adds first economic estimates of pollen costs and quantifies urban forest benefits; useful for policy design. Incremental for pollution literature but novel for forestry–health nexus.
Well-structured, transparent equations, rich figures, clear exposition. Dense appendix but overall argument easy to follow.
Remote-sensing data and shapefiles potentially shareable; however medical claims and some government GIS layers are restricted; code and digitised maps not yet publicly archived.
Urban forestry is globally widespread; results on pollution/pollen trade-off useful for many cities. Context-specific health care and planting species may limit direct transferability.
